questions.question: What is Go's error interface, and how does a type implement it?
questions.title: The error interface
questions.direct_answer: Go's built-in `error` type is an interface containing one method: `Error() string`. A value satisfies it automatically when its method set includes that method; no declaration or inheritance is required. The string explains the failure, while the concrete value may carry structured details.

interviewer_intent.testing: The built-in contract, implicit interface satisfaction, and the difference between message and structured identity.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating an error as only a string or forgetting that pointer and value method sets differ.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a small custom type and explain how callers inspect it through the error interface.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `error` is the predeclared interface `interface { Error() string }`.
Interface satisfaction is implicit; a type only needs the right method.
A nil `error` means success by convention.
The concrete error value may hold fields even though callers receive `error`.
Use `errors.Is` or `errors.As` for program decisions, not message matching.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Go's `error` type is a small built-in interface with one method, `Error() string`. Any concrete type whose method set contains that method satisfies `error` automatically, so there is no `implements` keyword. A successful operation conventionally returns a nil error; a failed operation returns a non-nil value that describes the failure.

The interface lets an API expose one stable return type while using different concrete errors underneath. The text from `Error` is useful for people and logs, but a struct can also retain fields such as an invalid field name, file path, or status code. Callers that need those details use `errors.As`, while callers that only need success or failure check `err != nil`.

For example, a `ValidationError` with `Field` and `Reason` fields can define `Error()` on a pointer receiver and be returned as `error`. Code can print it normally, yet a form handler can still extract the structured value and attach the message to the correct field.

The method receiver matters. If `Error` is defined on `*ValidationError`, only the pointer implements `error`; the non-pointer value does not. Error methods should also be safe and concise because formatting an error calls that method. In normal APIs I return the `error` interface, document meaningful error categories, and keep the concrete representation replaceable.

sections.title: One contract, many failure values
sections.content:
An interface value carries a dynamic type together with a dynamic value. Assigning `&ValidationError{...}` to an `error` therefore keeps both the fact that it is a `*ValidationError` and the data stored in that object. The static function signature remains simply `error`.

The `Error` method is the common display contract, not the complete data model. Equality, category checks, retry decisions, and user-facing translations should rely on stable error identity or type. This separation lets an error remain readable without forcing programs to parse prose.

sections.title: What an error value contains
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[ValidationError value] --> B[Error method]
  A --> C[Field and Reason data]
  B --> D[error interface]
  D --> E[Human-readable message]
  D --> F[errors.As finds concrete type]
  F --> C
```

questions.question: Why can a nil pointer returned as an error still be non-nil?
questions.title: The typed-nil error trap
questions.direct_answer: An interface is nil only when both its dynamic type and dynamic value are absent. Returning a typed nil pointer such as `(*MyError)(nil)` stores the type `*MyError` inside the error interface, so `err != nil` is true even though the pointer inside it is nil.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether interface nil semantics can be explained as a type-and-value pair.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning a nil `*CustomError` variable and expecting the resulting interface to be nil.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace the interface pair and show the explicit nil success return.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A nil interface has neither a dynamic type nor a dynamic value.
A typed nil pointer placed in `error` gives the interface a dynamic type.
That interface therefore compares unequal to nil.
Return plain `nil` on the success path.
Avoid returning a concrete pointer error type from an API signature.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Go interface is nil only when it contains no dynamic type and no dynamic value. A pointer variable can be nil while still having a concrete type such as `*ParseError`. When that pointer is converted to `error`, the interface stores the pair `(*ParseError, nil)`, so the interface itself is populated and `err == nil` is false.

For example, a function might declare `var problem *ParseError` and return `problem` on its success path. The caller sees a non-nil error even though the pointer held by the interface is nil. Printing or calling its `Error` method may also panic if the method dereferences the receiver.

The reliable pattern is to return the untyped `nil` value directly when no failure occurred, and construct the concrete error only inside the failing branch. It is also clearer for the function signature to return `error` rather than `*ParseError`; callers can still recover the concrete type with `errors.As`.

A nil-safe `Error` method does not change the comparison rule. It may prevent a panic during formatting, but the interface remains non-nil because its dynamic type is present. I treat this as an interface-representation issue and fix the return path, rather than adding special checks at every caller.

sections.title: Nil has two layers at an interface boundary
sections.content:
Think of an interface as a small box with a type label and a value slot. An empty box is nil. Putting a nil `*ParseError` into the box fills in the type label even though the value slot contains a nil pointer.

The caller compares the whole box with nil, not just the inner pointer. That is why the bug is best prevented where the interface is created: use an explicit `return nil` for success and return a real error object only for failure.

sections.title: Nil pointer versus nil interface
sections.content:
| Expression returned | Dynamic type | Dynamic value | `err == nil` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nil` | none | none | true |
| `(*ParseError)(nil)` | `*ParseError` | nil pointer | false |
| `&ParseError{...}` | `*ParseError` | non-nil pointer | false |

questions.question: Should a Go function return error or a concrete error type?
questions.title: Return error, preserve useful detail
questions.direct_answer: Most Go functions should return the `error` interface, not a concrete error pointer. This keeps the implementation flexible, avoids typed-nil surprises, and still allows callers to inspect documented concrete errors with `errors.As` or categories with `errors.Is`.

interviewer_intent.testing: API design, abstraction, and structured error inspection.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming a return type must be concrete for callers to access error details.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain which error identities are intentionally documented as stable API behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use `error` for the usual function return type.
Concrete error values can still carry structured fields.
Callers use `errors.As` to retrieve a documented concrete type.
Returning a concrete pointer can create typed-nil mistakes.
Exposing a type or sentinel makes it part of the API contract.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
In most APIs I return the built-in `error` interface. It gives every caller the same simple success check and lets the implementation choose a plain error, sentinel, wrapped cause, or custom type. Returning a concrete pointer ties the signature to one representation and makes a typed nil easier to return accidentally.

Returning `error` does not remove structured information. For example, a parser can return a `*SyntaxError` as an `error`. A basic caller prints the message, while a caller that needs the line number declares a target and uses `errors.As(err, &target)`. That search also works through wrapping layers.

The boundary is the public contract. If documentation promises that an operation returns a particular type or wraps a sentinel, callers may depend on that identity. Changing it later can break their branching logic even if the error message stays similar. Internal implementation failures should not be exposed automatically just because `%w` makes wrapping easy.

A concrete return can make sense in a tightly controlled internal helper whose only useful result is that structure, but it is unusual for general error reporting. My default is `error`, with documented types or sentinels only when callers have a real recovery decision to make.

sections.title: Concept guide · Return error, preserve useful detail
sections.content:
The return type answers what every caller must understand: the operation can fail. Documentation answers the narrower question of which failures callers may inspect. These are separate design decisions.

A package can add fields to an internal error, replace it with a sentinel, or attach context without changing a function signature that returns `error`. Once a concrete type or wrapped cause is promised publicly, however, preserving that behavior becomes part of compatibility.

sections.title: Choosing the return surface
sections.content:
| Return surface | Caller experience | Main cost |
|---|---|---|
| `error` | Simple nil check; `Is` and `As` when documented | Important identities need documentation |
| `*SyntaxError` | Fields are directly visible | Signature is coupled to one type; typed nil risk |
| `bool` or status only | Very small contract | Loses the reason and wrapping context |
